front: Trigger: sorted input + find a pair with some sum
back: Opposite ends, walk inward. Too small → left moves. Too big → right moves.

front: Trigger: "reads the same forward and backward"
back: Opposite ends. Compare the outside pair, step both inward.

front: Trigger: "in order, but not necessarily adjacent" across two sequences
back: Same direction, one pointer each. Fast one moves every step, slow one only on a match.

front: Trigger: pick two positions to maximize something capped by the smaller one
back: Start wide, move the weaker side inward.

front: Trigger: "find 3 numbers that sum to X"
back: Sort, fix one, two-pointer the other two. O(n²).

front: Trigger: prefix/suffix answer, but O(1) space required
back: Two pointers from the ends. Process the side whose bound is already known.

front: Trigger: sorted input with negatives, output must be sorted by size
back: Biggest magnitudes are at the ends. Fill the output from the back.

front: Two Sum II: why is it safe to discard numbers[left] when the sum is too small?
back: numbers[right] is the biggest partner still in play. If even it isn't enough, numbers[left] has no partner at all.

front: Two Sum II: why is it safe to discard numbers[right] when the sum is too big?
back: numbers[left] is the smallest partner left. If even it overshoots, numbers[right] has no partner.

front: Container: why move the SHORTER line?
back: Every container that keeps it is narrower and no taller, so none can beat the current area. It's finished.

front: Container: what if both lines are equal?
back: Move either. Neither can make a better container with the other.

front: Is Subsequence: why is greedy matching safe?
back: Matching a character at its earliest spot leaves the most of t for the rest.

front: Trapping water (two pointers): why can you finalize the side with the smaller max?
back: Its own max is exact, and the other side already has a taller bar. So the smaller max is the water level.

front: 3Sum: why sort first?
back:
• Lets the pair search use two pointers (O(n) per fixed number)
  • Puts duplicates next to each other so you can skip them

front: 3Sum: why break when nums[i] > 0?
back: Everything to its right is positive too. No triple can reach 0.

front: Why is the opposite-ends loop O(n)?
back: Every step discards at least one item. At most n steps.

front: LC 125 Valid Palindrome — key idea, trap
back:
• Two pointers; skip non-alphanumerics; compare .lower()
  • Trap: the skip loops need left < right too (try ".,!")
  • O(n), O(1)

front: LC 392 Is Subsequence — key idea
back:
• One pointer per string; i (in s) moves only on a match
  • Return i == len(s)
  • O(len t), O(1)

front: LC 167 Two Sum II — key idea, trap
back:
• Ends inward; too small → left, too big → right
  • Trap: return 1-indexed positions
  • O(n), O(1)

front: LC 977 Squares of a Sorted Array — key idea
back:
• Compare abs at both ends; bigger square goes in the last open slot
  • O(n) (vs O(n log n) square-then-sort)

front: LC 11 Container With Most Water — key idea
back:
• area = (right − left) × min(h[left], h[right])
  • Move the shorter side
  • O(n), O(1)

front: LC 15 3Sum — key idea, Big-O
back:
• Sort; for each i, Two Sum II on the rest for −nums[i]
  • Skip duplicates in 3 places
  • O(n²) time

front: LC 15 3Sum — the three duplicate skips
LC 16 3Sum Closest — key idea
back:
• Same loop as 3Sum; track best by abs(total − target)
  • Exact hit → return immediately
  • No duplicate skipping needed

front: LC 42 Trapping Rain Water — O(1) space version
back: Process the side with the smaller max.

front: Write the opposite-ends skeleton
while left < right vs while left <= right — how do you choose?
back: Ask: does a pointer meeting itself mean anything? Pairs need two different items → <. Trace 1- and 2-item inputs. (M5)

front: 3Sum: skip with nums[i] == nums[i - 1] or nums[i] == nums[i + 1]?
back: i - 1. The i + 1 version skips the first copy, so [-1, -1, 2] is lost.

front: 3Sum: what breaks if you don't skip after a match?
back: The same triple is recorded twice, e.g. [-2, 0, 2] in [-2, 0, 0, 2, 2].

front: Is Subsequence: what's wrong with t.find(ch) for each character of s?
back: It searches from the start each time, so it ignores order. Use t.find(ch, j) or two pointers.

front: Two Sum II with a dict: what's the problem?
back: It works, but uses O(n) space. The problem asks for O(1); the sorted order is the hint.

front: New bug type (lab 2.09): moving the wrong pointer
back: Too small but you move right → the sum gets smaller. Check: "Which pointer moves the sum the way I need?" (Candidate M8.)

front: Big-O of 3Sum by brute force vs two pointers
back: Brute: O(n³). Sort + two pointers: O(n²).
